Module 14 · Visualizing Statistical Relationships and Distributions¶

BUSN 3030E — Python Programming Skills for Business Analytics I

Learning objectives. After this module you will be able to

  • show the relationship between two numeric variables with scatter and line plots;
  • encode additional variables with color (hue), marker style (style), size (size), and small multiples (col, row);
  • visualize distributions with histograms, kernel density estimates, and ECDFs, and choose among them;
  • explore many variables at once with joint and pair plots;
  • label figures so that they can stand on their own in a report.

1 · Preparation¶

A good chart reveals patterns that a table of numbers hides. seaborn is a plotting library built on top of matplotlib that works directly with pandas DataFrames: you name the columns to put on each axis, and seaborn handles the rest.

In [1]:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

sns.set_theme() applies a clean default style to every figure. seaborn ships with example datasets, which sns.load_dataset() downloads from the web. We start with tips: 244 restaurant bills, with the tip, the size of the party, and details of the visit.

In [2]:
tips = sns.load_dataset("tips")
tips.head()
Out[2]:
total_bill tip sex smoker day time size
0 16.99 1.01 Female No Sun Dinner 2
1 10.34 1.66 Male No Sun Dinner 3
2 21.01 3.50 Male No Sun Dinner 3
3 23.68 3.31 Male No Sun Dinner 2
4 24.59 3.61 Female No Sun Dinner 4

1.1 Scatter plots¶

sns.relplot() (relational plot) draws the relationship between two numeric variables. By default it draws a scatter plot, one point per row.

In [3]:
sns.relplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip");

Larger bills come with larger tips. The semicolon at the end of the line suppresses a line of text output that would otherwise appear above the figure.

Adding variables with semantics. A third variable can be mapped to the color of the points with hue, and to their shape with style. Using both for the same variable makes the plot readable in black and white and for color-blind readers.

In [4]:
sns.relplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", hue="smoker", style="smoker");

When the hue variable is numeric, seaborn switches from distinct colors to a sequential palette. A numeric variable can also be mapped to the size of the points:

In [5]:
sns.relplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", hue="size", size="size", sizes=(20, 200));

Less is more. Each extra semantic makes a plot harder to read. Two or three variables per plot is usually the limit. Small multiples (§1.3) are often a better way to show more.

1.2 Line plots¶

When the x variable is time, or another continuous quantity with a natural order, a line plot emphasizes continuity. Set kind="line". The flights dataset records the monthly number of airline passengers (in thousands) from 1949 to 1960:

In [6]:
flights = sns.load_dataset("flights")
flights.head()
Out[6]:
year month passengers
0 1949 Jan 112
1 1949 Feb 118
2 1949 Mar 132
3 1949 Apr 129
4 1949 May 121
In [7]:
sns.relplot(data=flights, x="year", y="passengers", kind="line");

Each year has twelve observations, one per month. seaborn aggregates repeated measurements automatically: the line shows the mean, and the shaded band a 95% confidence interval for the mean. Mapping month to hue instead draws one line per month and reveals the seasonal pattern:

In [8]:
sns.relplot(data=flights, x="year", y="passengers", hue="month", kind="line", palette="viridis");

Passenger numbers grew every year, and summer months were always the busiest.

1.3 Small multiples with facets¶

To show how a relationship depends on a categorical variable, draw one panel per category with col (columns) and row (rows). These small multiples share their axes, which makes comparisons easy.

In [9]:
sns.relplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", hue="smoker", col="time");

Use col_wrap to wrap many panels into several rows, and height and aspect to set the size of each panel:

In [10]:
sns.relplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", col="day", col_wrap=2, height=3, aspect=1.2);

1.4 Labeling figures¶

A figure in a report must be understandable without the code that made it. seaborn's figure-level functions return a grid object; its methods set the axis labels and titles.

In [11]:
g = sns.relplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", hue="time")
g.set_axis_labels("Total bill ($)", "Tip ($)")
g.figure.suptitle("Tips rise with the size of the bill", y=1.03);

1.5 Histograms¶

Before modeling a variable, look at its distribution: its range, center, shape, and any outliers. sns.displot() (distribution plot) draws a histogram by default. The penguins dataset measures 344 penguins of three species:

In [12]:
penguins = sns.load_dataset("penguins")
penguins.head()
Out[12]:
species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex
0 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181.0 3750.0 Male
1 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 17.4 186.0 3800.0 Female
2 Adelie Torgersen 40.3 18.0 195.0 3250.0 Female
3 Adelie Torgersen NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN
4 Adelie Torgersen 36.7 19.3 193.0 3450.0 Female
In [13]:
sns.displot(data=penguins, x="flipper_length_mm");

The distribution has two peaks (it is bimodal), a hint that the data mix different groups.

Choosing the bins. The bin size can change the story. Check that your conclusions hold across a few choices with binwidth or bins:

In [14]:
sns.displot(data=penguins, x="flipper_length_mm", binwidth=3);

For a variable that takes a few whole-number values, such as party size, set discrete=True to center one bar on each value:

In [15]:
sns.displot(data=tips, x="size", discrete=True);

Comparing groups. Mapping a variable to hue draws one histogram per group. The bimodal shape turns out to come from the species:

In [16]:
sns.displot(data=penguins, x="flipper_length_mm", hue="species");

Overlapping bars can be hard to read. element="step" draws outlines, and multiple="stack" stacks the groups:

In [17]:
sns.displot(data=penguins, x="flipper_length_mm", hue="species", multiple="stack");

When groups have very different sizes, compare their shapes rather than their counts: stat="density" with common_norm=False scales each group's histogram separately.

In [18]:
sns.displot(data=penguins, x="flipper_length_mm", hue="species",
            stat="density", common_norm=False, element="step");

1.6 Kernel density estimates¶

A kernel density estimate (KDE) replaces the bars with a smooth curve. It is often easier to compare several groups with KDEs than with histograms.

In [19]:
sns.displot(data=penguins, x="flipper_length_mm", hue="species", kind="kde", fill=True);

The smoothness is controlled by bw_adjust (bandwidth): smaller values follow the data more closely, larger values smooth more.

In [20]:
sns.displot(data=penguins, x="flipper_length_mm", kind="kde", bw_adjust=0.5);

KDE pitfalls. A KDE always draws a smooth curve, even where the data are not smooth, and it can spill into impossible values. A restaurant bill cannot be negative, yet the curve below extends below zero. cut=0 stops the curve at the extreme data points.

In [21]:
sns.displot(data=tips, x="total_bill", kind="kde");

A good compromise is a histogram with a KDE curve on top (kde=True):

In [22]:
sns.displot(data=tips, x="total_bill", kde=True);

1.7 Empirical cumulative distributions¶

An ECDF plots, for each value, the proportion of observations at or below it. It has no bins or bandwidth to choose, and reading quantiles off it is easy: the x-value where the curve crosses 0.5 is the median.

In [23]:
sns.displot(data=penguins, x="flipper_length_mm", hue="species", kind="ecdf");

1.8 Two variables, many variables¶

displot() also accepts a y variable, producing a two-dimensional histogram or KDE:

In [24]:
sns.displot(data=penguins, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", hue="species", kind="kde");

sns.jointplot() combines a bivariate plot with the distribution of each variable along the margins:

In [25]:
sns.jointplot(data=penguins, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", hue="species");

sns.pairplot() draws every pairwise scatter plot of the numeric columns, with each variable's distribution on the diagonal. It is a quick first look at a new dataset.

In [26]:
sns.pairplot(data=penguins, hue="species", height=2);

1.9 Choosing a plot¶

Question Plot
How are two numeric variables related? scatter: relplot(x=, y=)
How does a variable change over time? line: relplot(x=, y=, kind="line")
How is one variable distributed? displot(x=) (histogram, kind="kde", kind="ecdf")
Does the relationship differ across groups? add hue=, or facet with col= / row=
What does a new dataset look like? pairplot(data)

2 · Warmup¶

Exercise 2.1. Load the Gapminder data (Module 12) and relate GDP per capita to life expectancy with a scatter plot.

In [27]:
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hanisaf/python-programming-skills/main/data/"
gapminder = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gapminder.tsv", sep="\t")

sns.relplot(data=gapminder, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp");

Most countries are crowded on the left, because GDP per capita is highly skewed: a few countries are far richer than the rest. A logarithmic scale spreads them out and reveals a roughly linear relationship.

In [28]:
g = sns.relplot(data=gapminder, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", hue="continent")
g.set(xscale="log")
g.set_axis_labels("GDP per capita (log scale, inflation-adjusted $)", "Life expectancy (years)");

Exercise 2.2. Show only the year 2007, and map population to the size of the points.

In [29]:
g = sns.relplot(data=gapminder[gapminder["year"] == 2007],
                x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", hue="continent", size="pop", sizes=(20, 800), alpha=0.7)
g.set(xscale="log")
g.set_axis_labels("GDP per capita (log scale)", "Life expectancy (years)");

alpha makes the points partly transparent, so that overlapping bubbles remain visible. This plot is the famous Gapminder bubble chart.

Exercise 2.3. Use small multiples to compare 1952, 1977, and 2007.

In [30]:
g = sns.relplot(data=gapminder[gapminder["year"].isin([1952, 1977, 2007])],
                x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", hue="continent", col="year", height=3.5)
g.set(xscale="log");

Exercise 2.4. How did life expectancy evolve on each continent?

In [31]:
g = sns.relplot(data=gapminder, x="year", y="lifeExp", hue="continent", kind="line")
g.set_axis_labels("Year", "Life expectancy (years)");

Life expectancy rose on every continent; Africa's progress stalled in the 1990s.

Exercise 2.5. Compare the distribution of life expectancy across continents in 2007.

In [32]:
sns.displot(data=gapminder[gapminder["year"] == 2007], x="lifeExp", hue="continent",
            kind="kde", fill=True, common_norm=False, cut=0);

3 · Workout¶

Return to the insurance data from Module 13.

In [33]:
insurance = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "insurance.csv")

Exercise 3.1. Draw a scatter plot matrix of all numeric variables, colored by smoking status. Which relationships stand out?

In [34]:
sns.pairplot(data=insurance, hue="smoker", height=2.2);

Smokers are charged more at every age, and the age–charges panel shows three distinct bands of points. The distribution of charges is strongly skewed to the right.

Exercise 3.2. Focus on BMI and charges. Is the relationship different for smokers and non-smokers?

In [35]:
sns.jointplot(data=insurance, x="bmi", y="charges", hue="smoker");

For non-smokers, BMI barely matters. For smokers, charges jump sharply around a BMI of 30, the clinical threshold for obesity.

Exercise 3.3. Does the pattern differ between women and men? Use KDE contours and facets.

In [36]:
g = sns.displot(data=insurance, x="bmi", y="charges", hue="smoker", col="sex", kind="kde")
g.set_axis_labels("Body mass index", "Annual charges ($)");

The pattern is the same for women and men, which agrees with the small, non-significant coefficient of sex in the regression of Module 13. The visualization also shows something the linear regression missed: the effect of BMI depends on smoking status (an interaction).

Summary¶

Function Draws Key options
sns.relplot() scatter or line plots hue, style, size, col, row, kind="line"
sns.displot() histograms, KDEs, ECDFs binwidth, bins, discrete, kind, multiple, stat, common_norm
sns.jointplot() bivariate plot with marginal distributions kind, hue
sns.pairplot() all pairwise relationships hue, vars, height
grid methods labels and scales g.set_axis_labels(), g.set(xscale="log"), g.figure.suptitle()
